title: Every act an offering
hookLine: one stretch of sound holds four words, and Arjuna asks why he can't just stop
carry: every act can be an offering to god
tomorrow: Sam wants a Sanskrit tattoo for graduation. good idea?
last: THE ACT IS YOURS, NEVER THE FRUIT.

cards: Say did you eat yet, fast, to a friend across a kitchen, and it comes out as one long slur. Sanskrit writes that slur down.
The first stretch of Nani's line, karmanyevadhikaraste, sits under one unbroken head line, and inside it are four words: karmani, in action; eva, only; adhikarah, the right; te, yours.
Their edges melted as they were said, and the grammarians call that melting sandhi, joining. One stretch of sound you can't pull apart without breaking it.
Arjuna is about to learn that a life and its actions are like that too.

teach.b: In the Gita's third chapter, Arjuna pushes back. If knowing is higher than doing, he asks Krishna, why are you urging me into this terrible act?
It's a very human question: if acting gets you tangled, why not step back from all of it? Krishna's answer: you can't.

teach.h: NO ONE STAYS A MOMENT WITHOUT ACTING.
teach.b: No one can stay even a moment without acting, he says, and even keeping a body alive takes action. Simply not starting work sets no one free. So the real question isn't whether to act.
It's how. And here Krishna hands over one of the Gita's great keys.
Action binds, he says, except action done as yajna, as an offering.

teach.h: WHATEVER YOU DO, OFFER IT TO ME.
teach.b: Later he says it to Arjuna plainly: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, do it as an offering to me.

That's why, in many Hindu homes, food is set before God before anyone eats, and comes back as prasad, a blessed gift. It's why some people end a task or a meal with a short line: Krishnarpanam, offered to Krishna.
The work doesn't change. What it's for changes. Many teachers read this as the other half of yesterday's verse: you let go of the fruit by giving it away before it arrives.
Like the words in sandhi, the act and the offering are said in one breath.

how: In many Hindu homes food is offered to God (naivedya) before it is eaten and then shared as prasad; some people close an act or a meal with 'Krishnarpanam' or 'Sri Krishnarpanam astu', offered to Krishna. Sanskrit readers learn to undo sandhi to find the words in a joined run.

a script that writes joined words just as they're said
a script where each word has its own color

games.q: action and offering — tap the pairs.
p: food offered to God, then shared

s: Krishna tells Arjuna to escape karma by doing nothing at all
no one stays a moment without acting. the key is acting as an offering.
in many Hindu homes, food is offered to God before anyone eats
it comes back as prasad, a blessed gift.
karmanyevadhikaraste is one long rare word
four words joined by sandhi: in action, only, the right, yours.

games.q: your aunt sets a plate before the shrine and only then serves dinner. a cousin asks why. what fits the Gita?
o: Krishna asks that whatever you eat or do be offered to him first.
it brings luck, so the food turns out better.
it's old manners; nobody really knows why.
games.why: whatever you do, eat, offer or give, make it an offering: the food comes back as prasad.

practice: Bring to mind one ordinary thing you'll do today: a meal, a shift, homework, a call home. Breathe slowly and, if you pray, offer it before you start, in your own words or with the old line, Krishnarpanam, offered to Krishna.
If you don't pray, offer it to someone it will help. Then sit, and let the task feel a little less like yours alone.

wordCard.voice: Devanagari: a script where one head line can hold several words, joined by sandhi just as they're said.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sacrifice, offering; in the Gita, action done as an offering, which doesn't bind.

carryVoice: Pocket this: every act can be an offering to God, the meal, the work, the day. Rest well.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.1–3.9 (Arjuna's question; no one stays a moment without acting; action binds except when done as yajna)
Bhagavad Gita 9.27 ('whatever you do, eat, offer, give… do it as an offering to me')
